subject: Animation
title: Chicken Run: Aardman Goes Feature-Length
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Chicken Run: Aardman Goes Feature-Length.

hook.text: In 2000, Aardman released Chicken Run, a stop-motion film about chickens escaping a pie-making farm.

buildup.text: The film was a DreamWorks co-production and the most ambitious clay animation project ever attempted.

discovery.text: Chicken Run earned $224 million worldwide and became the highest-grossing stop-motion film at the time.

twist.text: DreamWorks wanted a sequel immediately. Aardman refused to rush and the partnership eventually dissolved.

climax.text: Chicken Run proved that stop-motion could compete with CGI at the box office when the story was right.

punchline.text: Clay chickens outearned most computer-animated films.

quiz.question: What milestone did Chicken Run achieve for stop-motion?
options: It was the first stop-motion film ever
It became the highest-grossing stop-motion film at the time, proving the format could compete
It won the Academy Award for Best Picture

details.summary: Chicken Run (2000) was Aardman's first feature film and the highest-grossing stop-motion movie at the time. It proved clay animation could sustain a 90-minute story and compete with CGI blockbusters at the box office.
details.whyItMatters: Chicken Run demonstrated that stop-motion could work at feature scale, not just in shorts. It opened the door for other studios to invest in full-length stop-motion films.
takeaways: Chicken Run was Aardman's first and hugely successful feature film
It proved stop-motion could sustain feature-length storytelling
The film earned over $224 million worldwide against a modest budget

faq.question: What challenges did Aardman face making a feature-length film?
faq.answer: Scaling from 30-minute shorts to 90 minutes required bigger sets, more animators, and complex production scheduling. They animated at roughly 3 seconds of footage per animator per day.

faq.question: Why was Chicken Run compared to The Great Escape?
faq.answer: The film deliberately references the 1963 prisoner-of-war classic, casting chickens as inmates plotting escape from a farm. The comedic homage gave adults a layer of enjoyment beyond the family-friendly surface.
